'''Yilan Creole'''{{efn|{{langx|ja|寒渓語|Kankei-go}}; {{lang-zh|t=寒溪語|p=Hánxīyǔ}}}} is a [[Japanese-based creole languages|Japanese-based creole]] spoken in four villages in southern [[Yilan County, Taiwan]]. It arose in the 1930s and 1940s through contact between Japanese colonists and the indigenous [[Atayal people]] of the area. The vocabulary of a speaker born in 1974 was 70% [[Japanese language|Japanese]] and 30% [[Atayal language|Atayal]], but the grammar of the [[Creole language|creole]] does not closely resemble either of the source languages.<ref name="2010 Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages">{{cite journal|last1=Chien|first1=Yuehchen|last2=Sanada|first2=Shinji|date=2010|title=Yilan Creole in Taiwan|journal=Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages|volume=25|number=2|pages=350–357|doi=10.1075/jpcl.25.2.11yue}}</ref>

Yilan Creole is [[Mutual intelligibility|mutually unintelligible]] with both Japanese and Atayal.<ref name="Qiu 2015">{{Cite thesis |last=Qiu |first=P. |title=A Preliminary Investigation of Yilan Creole in Taiwan: Discussing Predicate Position in Yilan Creole |date=2015 |degree=Master's |publisher=University of Alberta |url=https://era.library.ualberta.ca/files/02870z43h/Qiu_Peng_201502_MA.pdf |doi=10.7939/R3930P347 |doi-access=free |language=en}}</ref> The creole was identified in 2006 by Chien Yuehchen and Sanada Shinji, but its existence is still largely unknown.<ref name="Qiu 2015" /><ref name="Sanada Chien">{{Cite journal |last1=Chien |first1=Yuehchen 簡月真 |last2=Sanada |first2=Shinji 真田信治 |date=2010 |title=Dōng Táiwān Tàiyǎzú de Yílán kèlǐàoěr |script-title=zh:東台灣泰雅族的宜蘭克里奧爾 spoken language in Taiwan, threatens the existence of Yilan Creole.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

== Classification ==
Yilan Creole is a creole language that is considered to be part of the [[Japonic languages|Japonic language family]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Yilan Creole Japanese |url=http://glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/yila1234 |access-date=March 10, 2017 |website=Glottolog |language=en}}</ref> The superstratum and substratum languages of the creole are Japanese and Atayal, respectively.<ref name="Qiu 2015" /> It is based on Japanese vocabulary and grammar, while simultaneously integrating the phonology, vocabulary, and grammar of the underlying Atayal or Sediq languages. It also absorbed some Hokkien and Mandarin vocabulary,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yuehchen |first=Chien |last2=Shinji |first2=Sanada |date=2010-08-16 |title=Yilan Creole in Taiwan |url=http://www.jbe-platform.com/content/journals/10.1075/jpcl.25.2.11yue |journal=Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages |language=en |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=350–357 |doi=10.1075/jpcl.25.2.11yue |issn=0920-9034|url-access=subscription }}</ref> ultimately crystallizing into a new language through [[Fossilization (linguistics)|linguistic fossilization]]. It has possibly been used as a first language among the Atayal and Seediq people since the 1930s.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

== History ==
During [[Taiwan under Japanese rule]] period under the [[Treaty of Shimonoseki|Shimonoseki Treaty]] of 1895 until 1945.<ref name="Vestiges">{{Cite book |last=Homma |first=N. |title=Ningen Bunka Gakubu Gakusei Ronbun-shū Dai 11-gō |date=2013 |publisher=Kyōto Gakuen Daigaku Ningen Bunka Gakubu |editor-last=Kyōto Gakuen Daigaku Ningen Bunka Gakkai |editor-mask=Kyōto Gakuen Daigaku Ningen Bunka Gakkai 京都学園大学人間文化学会 |pages=222–227 |language=en |script-title=ja:人間文化学部学生論文集 第11号 |chapter=Vestiges of Japanese Colonialism in Taiwan |access-date=December 25, 2019 |editor-last2=Gakusei Ronbun-shū Henshū Iinkai |editor-mask2=Gakusei Ronbun-shū Henshū Iinkai 学生論文集編集委員会 |chapter-url=https://human.kyotogakuen.ac.jp/pdf/association/2012/i2012_05.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191225083032/https://human.kyotogakuen.ac.jp/pdf/association/2012/i2012_05.pdf |archive-date=December 25, 2019}}</ref><ref name="Parker 2012">{{Cite conference |last=Parker |first=J. D. |date=2012 |title=Japanese Language Education in Colonized Taiwan: Language and Assimilation |url=http://citation.allacademic.com/meta/p556741_index.html |conference=Paper presented at the annual meeting of the 56th Annual Conference of the Comparative and International Education Society, Caribe Hilton, San Juan, Puerto Rico |language=en |access-date=December 12, 2014 |url-status=}}{{dead link|date=September 2023}}</ref> Control over the island lasted about fifty years.<ref name="Vestiges" /> During the latter period of this time, [[Empire of Japan|Imperial Japan]] enforced Taiwanese [[Cultural assimilation|assimilation]] to Japanese language and culture.<ref name="Vestiges" /> As a result of this contact between the [[Atayal language|Atayal]] and [[Japanese language|Japanese]] languages, Yilan Creole surfaced.<ref name="Sanada Chien" /> Taiwanese people began attending schools taught in Japanese where all non-Japanese languages were banned, and by 1944 over 77% of Taiwanese were capable in speaking Japanese.<ref name="Parker 2012" /><ref name="Vestiges" /> Language reforms, name changes, and laws regarding social customs were among the reforms instilled by the Japanese Imperial government.<ref name="Vestiges" /> Many are still competent in Japanese today where it is sometimes used as a [[lingua franca]].<ref name="NINJAL">{{Cite web |title=Formation Processes of Japanese Language Varieties and Creoles |url=http://www.ninjal.ac.jp/english/research/project/a/creoles/ |access-date=March 10, 2017 |website=National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Qiu 2015" /> Although China attempted to rid influence of Japan in Taiwan after the [[surrender of Japan]] in 1945, the impact on language and culture in Taiwan is still largely evident.<ref name="Vestiges" />
[[File:Taiwan ROC political division map Yilan County.svg|thumb|Yilan County, Taiwan]]
Atayal features surfaced in the Japanese language spoken in Taiwan, eventually becoming a [[pidgin]] before it fully developed into a [[Creole language|creole]], and the language is now currently the only known Japanese-based creole on the island, and possibly in the world.<ref name="Qiu 2015" /><ref name="Chien 2015" />

== Contemporary usage ==
During the 2001 Indigenous Language Proficiency Test,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yuehchen |first=Chien |last2=Shinji |first2=Sanada |date=2010-08-16 |title=Yilan Creole in Taiwan |url=http://www.jbe-platform.com/content/journals/10.1075/jpcl.25.2.11yue |journal=Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages |language=en |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=350–357 |doi=10.1075/jpcl.25.2.11yue |issn=0920-9034|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Yilan Creole were excluded as non-indigenous languages. After vigorous advocacy by residents, they were finally recognized as "Hansi Atayal" and included in the proficiency test as a dialect of the Atayal language. During field interviews in 2009, residents self-identified their language as "Japanese".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Heinrich |first=Patrick |title=Routledge handbook of Japanese sociolinguistics |last2=Ōhara |first2=Yumiko |date=2019 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-79027-7 |series=Routledge handbooks |location=Abingdon, Oxon New York, NY}}</ref>

== Geographic distribution ==
The [[Creole language|creole]] is spoken in [[Yilan County, Taiwan|Yilan County]] in Eastern Taiwan, mainly in Tungyueh Village (東岳村) and Chinyang Village (金洋村), both of which are in [[Datong, Yilan|Datong Township]] (大同鄉); and Aohua Village (澳花村), and Hanhsi Village (寒溪村), both of which are in [[Nan'ao, Yilan|Nan'ao Township]] (南澳鄉).

The [[Variety (linguistics)|varieties]] spoken in each village contain some minor differences.<ref name="Chien 2015" /><ref name="Sanada Chien" /> Although the exact number of Yilan Creole speakers is unknown, it is likely less than the total population of the four villages, which is 3,000.<ref name="Chien 2015" /><ref name="Qiu 2015" /> One estimate is that 2,000 to 3,000 speakers of Yilan Creole currently exist.<ref name="Qiu 2015" /> While the creole is currently used among all generations,<ref name="NINJAL" /> younger generations are receiving less exposure to it, causing the language to become [[Endangered language|endangered]].<ref name="Sanada Chien" /> While older speakers may not be fluent in [[Mandarin Chinese|Mandarin]], younger generations are consistently using Mandarin more.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

The Japanese language still has some influence in Taiwan society today. Websites in Japanese are regularly viewed by Taiwanese, with "few other countries [producing] as much information in Japanese as Taiwan".<ref name="Vestiges" /> Evidence of Japanese signboards, particularly with the use of the Japanese [[hiragana]] character の (''no'') can often be seen in Taiwan.<ref name="Vestiges" /> Taiwanese citizens who received Japanese education during the annexation of the nation still speak Japanese fluently today.<ref name="Vestiges" /> There are three generations of Yilan Creole speakers, with the older and middle generations using the creole significantly more than the younger generation.<ref name="Qiu 2015" />

In Tungyueh Village, younger generations are generally not fluent in Yilan Creole, while there are still fluent younger generation speakers of the Creole in Aohua.<ref name="Chien 2015" /> After a push for preserving a more traditional and pure sense of [[Atayal people|Atayal heritage]], Yilan Creole that is imbued with Japanese features was removed from language examinations. This further instilled a tendency toward Mandarin and a push away from Yilan Creole in young speakers.<ref name="Qiu 2015" /> While older generations prefer to speak Japanese or Yilan Creole with people of the same age, they will often use Atayal or Mandarin mixed with Yilan Creole when speaking with younger generations; younger generations will similarly prefer Mandarin with same-age speakers, but may use Yilan Creole with older generations.<ref name="Qiu 2015" />

Due to the migration of Japanese from western Japan to Taiwan in the early half of the twentieth century, with seventy percent of Taiwan's immigrants being from western Japan (such as from [[Kyushu]] and [[Okinawa Islands|Okinawa]]), Yilan Creole acquired some features of the dialects of western Japan. However, speakers are generally unaware that they are regional rather than standard Japanese features.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

Consonants in Yilan Creole are mostly identical to those of Atayal but it lacks the [[Uvular consonant|uvular]] [[Stop consonant|stop]] /q/. It acquired the [[Voice (phonetics)|voiced]] stop /d/ from Japanese, which is only found in loanwords.<ref name="Sanada Chien" />

=== Vowels ===
Yilan Creole [[vowel]]s consist of /a/, /i/, /u/, /e/ and /o/ which derive from both Japanese and Atayal, but also /ə/, which is inherited from Atayal.<ref name="Qiu 2015" /> The rounding of /u/ in Yilan Creole is that of the protrusion of [u] in Atayal, as opposed to the compression of {{IPA|[ɯᵝ]}} in Standard Japanese.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

Long consonants and vowels from Japanese words are often shortened in Yilan Creole, where ''gakkō'' 'school' in Japanese becomes ''gako'' 'school' in Yilan Creole.<ref name="Qiu 2015" />

=== Stress ===
[[Stress (linguistics)|Stress]] in Yilan Creole falls on the final syllable as it does in the Atayal language.<ref name="Qiu 2015" />

== Grammar ==

=== Morphology ===
Although Yilan Creole verbs are derived from Japanese and Atayal, [[Grammatical conjugation|verb conjugation]] patterns uniquely differ in some aspects. [[Tense–aspect–mood|Tense]] is noted through the use of [[affix]]es and temporal adverbs together. Atayal-based verbs will still use Japanese affixation.<ref name="Qiu 2015" /> Some processes of negation in Yilan Creole use Japanese derived forms to accommodate the [[realis mood]] that is part of Atayal grammar.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chien |first1=Yuehchen |last2=Sanada |first2=Shinji |date=2011 |title=Negation in Taiwan's Yilan Creole: Focusing on -Nay and -Ng |url=http://www.ls-japan.org/modules/documents/index.php?content_id=2222 |journal=Gengo kenkyū |language=en |issue=140 |pages=73–87 |id={{INIST|25353712}} |script-journal=ja:言語研究 |archive-date=2023-02-06 |access-date=2021-01-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206060457/https://www.ls-japan.org/modules/documents/index.php?content_id=2222 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Syntax ===
The [[word order]] of Yilan Creole is [[subject–object–verb word order|subject–object–verb]] (SOV). It follows Japanese sentence structure, but there is evidence of Mandarin-based [[subject–verb–object word order|subject–verb–object]] (SVO) sentences as well, particularly among younger speakers.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

== Vocabulary ==
In Yilan Creole, phonological forms of words are derived from Japanese, while the [[Semantics|semantic]] properties are derived from Atayal.<ref name="Chien 2015" /> According to a study on Yilan Creole in Tungyueh Village by  Zeitoun, Teng, and Wu, "the proportion of Atayal-derived words in the Yilan Creole basic vocabulary is 18.3%, and that of Japanese-derived words is 35.6%. Both Atayal-derived words and Japanese-derived words can be used for 33.8% of the items".<ref name="Chien 2015" /> [[Mandarin Chinese|Mandarin]] and [[Southern Min]] words also exist, but far less. Older generation speakers tend to use Atayal and Japanese variants more often than younger generational speakers, who prefer Mandarin variants, when they exist. Mandarin based words lose their tone in Yilan Creole.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

Many Atayal words relating to nature, animals, and plants survived in the creole. Vocabulary of most concepts such as these related to traditional [[Atayal people|Atayal]] and [[Seediq people|Seediq]] life and culture are retained in Yilan Creole.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

=== Suffixes ===
The verb [[suffix]] {{lang|crp-TW|-suru}} in Yilan Creole, derived from the Japanese verb 'to do', is similar to its Japanese counterpart, except in that it is a [[Bound and free morphemes|bound morpheme]], while the Japanese {{Transliteration|ja|-suru}} can stand alone as an [[Bound and free morphemes|independent verb]].<ref name="Chien 2015" /> Also, Yilan Creole {{lang|crp-TW|–suru}} can attach to nouns, adjectives, and, among young generational speakers, verbs. However, older generation speakers do not accept verbs + -''suru'' combinations.

Another affix in Yilan Creole is the Japanese derived {{lang|crp-TW|-rasyeru}} for [[causative]] forms. However, while Japanese [[inflection]] differs between consonant versus vowel ending verbs, the Yilan Creole suffix does not.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

=== Compound words ===
There are four types of [[Compound (linguistics)|compound words]] in Yilan Creole:<ref name="Chien 2015" />

# Type 1: Atayal-derived word + Atayal-derived word (e.g., ''hopa''-''la'i'')
# Type 2: Atayal-derived word + Japanese-derived word (e.g., ''hopa''-''tenki'')
# Type 3: Japanese-derived word + Atayal-derived word (e.g., ''naka''-''lukus'', ''kako''-''balay'')
# Type 4: Japanese-derived word + Japanese-derived word (e.g., ''naka''-''pangcyu'', ''unme''-''zyoto'')

While Type 1 compound words occur in Atayal, Japanese does not have occurrences of Type 4 compound words in its own language, suggesting that Type 2, 3, and 4 compound words are creations of Yilan Creole.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

The forms of pronouns are Japanese derived. However, in comparison to both Atayal and Japanese, Yilan Creole has a simplified pronominal system. The creole distinguishes pronouns between [[Grammatical person|person]] and [[Grammatical number|number]]. Yilan does not distinguish between [[Grammatical case|case]], bound or free pronouns, nor [[Clusivity|inclusive]] versus [[Clusivity|exclusive]] pronouns as Atayal does. It also does not distinguish between [[Grammatical gender|gender]] and [[Politeness and respect (Japanese language)|degree of politeness]] as Japanese does.<ref name="Chien 2015" />

=== Demonstratives ===
[[Demonstrative (linguistics)|Demonstratives]] in Yilan Creole are derived from Japanese.<ref name="Qiu 2015" />

=== Adjectives and adverbs ===
[[Adjective]]s and [[adverb]]s in Yilan Creole are derived from both Japanese and Atayal.<ref name="Qiu 2015" /> Atayal adjectives are primarily used for colors and subjective feelings. Unlike Japanese, adjectives in the creole languages are not inflected and tense is expressed through temporal adverbs.<ref name="Qiu 2015" /> Adjectives in Yilan Creole may also act as adverbs when modifying verbs. For example, the word ''lokah'' 'good, strong' "functions as an adjective when describing ''anta'' 'you' in the phrase ''lokah anta'' 'you (are) strong' ... while ''lokah'' functions as an adverb as in ''lokah benkyo'' 'to study hard'".<ref name="Qiu 2015" />

== Writing system ==
The [[Latin script|Latin]]-based [[writing system]] of Yilan Creole uses the Atayal writing system used in Taiwan.
